In [[number theory]], the '''Pólya conjecture''' (or '''Pólya's conjecture''') stated that "most" (i.e., 50% or more) of the [[natural number]]s [[less than]] any given number have an ''odd'' number of [[prime factor]]s. The [[conjecture]] was set forth by the Hungarian mathematician [[George Pólya]] in 1919,<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Pólya |first=G. |authorlink=George Pólya
 |date=1919
 |title=Verschiedene Bemerkungen zur Zahlentheorie |language=German
 |journal=[[Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung]]
 |jfm=47.0882.06
 |volume=28 |pages=31–40
}}</ref> and proven false in 1958 by [[C. Brian Haselgrove]]. Though mathematicians typically refer to this statement as the Pólya conjecture, Pólya never actually conjectured that the statement was true; rather, he showed that the truth of the statement would imply the [[Riemann hypothesis]]. For this reason, it is more accurately called "'''Pólya's problem'''". 

The size of the smallest [[counterexample]] is often used to demonstrate the fact that a conjecture can be true for many cases and still fail to hold in general,<ref>{{cite book |last=Stein |first=Sherman K.|authorlink= Sherman K. Stein |date=2010 |title=Mathematics: The Man-Made Universe |publisher=Courier Dover Publications |isbn=9780486404509 |page=483 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Kgv8xw7OCmgC&pg=PA483}}.</ref> providing an illustration of the [[strong law of small numbers]].

==Statement==
The Pólya conjecture states that for any <math>n>1</math>, if the [[natural numbers]] less than or equal to <math>n</math> (excluding 0) are partitioned into those with an ''odd'' number of prime factors and those with an ''even'' number of prime factors, then the former set has at least as many members as the latter set. Repeated prime factors are counted repeatedly; for instance, we say that 18 = 2&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;3&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;3 has an odd number of prime factors, while 60 = 2&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;2&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;3&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;5 has an even number of prime factors.

Equivalently, it can be stated in terms of the summatory [[Liouville function]], with the conjecture being that

:<math>L(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n \lambda(k) \leq 0 </math>

for all <math>n>1</math>. Here, <math>\lambda(k)=(-1)^{\Omega(k)}</math>, where <math>\Omega(k)</math> counts the total number of prime factors of <math>k</math>. Thus <math>\lambda(k)</math> is positive if the number of prime factors of <math>k</math> is even, and is negative if it is odd.

==Disproof==
The Pólya conjecture was disproven by [[C. Brian Haselgrove]] in 1958. He showed that the conjecture has a counterexample, which he estimated to be around 1.845&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;10<sup>361</sup>.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Haselgrove | first = C. B. | authorlink = C. Brian Haselgrove
 | date = 1958
 | title = A disproof of a conjecture of Pólya
 | journal = [[Mathematika]]
| issn=0025-5793
 | doi = 10.1112/S0025579300001480
 | mr = 0104638 | zbl=0085.27102 
 | volume = 5 | issue = 2 | pages = 141–145
}}</ref>

A (much smaller) explicit counterexample, of ''n'' = 906,180,359 was given by [[R. Sherman Lehman]] in 1960;<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Lehman |first=R. S.
 |date=1960
 |title=On Liouville's function
 |journal=[[Mathematics of Computation]]
 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1960-0120198-5 | doi-access=free
 |mr=0120198
 |jstor=2003890
 |volume=14 |issue=72 |pages=311–320}}</ref> the smallest counterexample is ''n'' = 906,150,257, found by Minoru Tanaka in 1980.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Tanaka |first=M. 
 |date=1980 
 |title=A Numerical Investigation on Cumulative Sum of the Liouville Function
 |journal=[[Tokyo Journal of Mathematics]]
 |doi=10.3836/tjm/1270216093
 |mr=0584557
 |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=187–189
|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The conjecture fails to hold for most values of ''n'' in the region of 906,150,257 &le; ''n'' &le; 906,488,079. In this region, the summatory [[Liouville function]] reaches a maximum value of 829 at ''n'' = 906,316,571.

Peter Humphries showed that
:<math>\liminf_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{L(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\le -1.389278414\cdots,\quad \limsup_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{L(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\ge 0.061867262\cdots.</math>{{refn|group=n|See Humphries<ref name="Humphries">{{cite journal |last1=Humphries |first1=Peter |title=The distribution of weighted sums of the Liouville function and Pólyaʼs conjecture |journal=Journal of Number Theory |date=February 2013 |volume=133 |issue=2 |pages=545-582 |doi=10.1016/j.jnt.2012.08.011 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1108.1524 }}</ref>, Theorem 2.3.}}

He also showed that assuming certain hypotheses including the [[Riemann hypothesis]], the set of numbers <math>n</math> such that <math>L(n)>0</math> has logarithm density <math>0<\delta\le\dfrac{1}{2}</math>.{{refn|group=n|See Humphries<ref name="Humphries" />, Theorem 1.5.}} A heuristic argument suggests that this set has logarithm density of around 0.00012.{{refn|group=n|See Humphries<ref name="Humphries" />, Section 7, p. 28.}}
